S01.name: Subacromial Pain Syndrome (Impingement)
keyExams: Subacromial cluster: Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer's, painful arc, Empty Can

Painful arc on elevation.text: Pain confined to roughly 60–120° of abduction marks the zone where the greater tuberosity and its attached supraspinatus tendon/subacromial bursa pass directly beneath the coracoacromial arch; pain easing again above ~120° as the tuberosity clears the arch is the classic mechanical signature of subacromial compression.
Painful arc on elevation.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter; Physiopedia, Painful Arc

subtle scapular dyskinesis.text: Delayed or reduced scapular upward rotation limits the normal elevation of the acromion during arm raise, further narrowing the subacromial outlet — Kibler's scapular dyskinesis framework identifies this as both a contributor to and consequence of impingement.
subtle scapular dyskinesis.source: Kibler, Scapular Dyskinesis and Its Relation to Shoulder Injury

no wasting.text: Preserved muscle bulk indicates an intact, mechanically-irritated cuff rather than the denervation/disuse atrophy expected with a structural full-thickness tear (S03) — a key differentiator between impingement and cuff tear on inspection alone.
no wasting.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

Forward head / rounded shoulders.text: Thoracic kyphosis with protracted, anteriorly-tilted scapulae (driven by a tight pectoralis minor) measurably reduces the acromiohumeral distance during elevation, a well-documented postural contributor to subacromial impingement.
Forward head / rounded shoulders.source: JOSPT Clinical Practice Guidelines, Shoulder Pain; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment

scapular downward rotation.text: Insufficient scapular upward rotation — from serratus anterior/lower trapezius underactivity — fails to lift the acromion clear of the humeral head's path during elevation, directly narrowing the subacromial space; this is the postural correlate of the 'upper-trap dominant' scapulohumeral-rhythm finding.
scapular downward rotation.source: Kibler, Scapular Dyskinesis and Its Relation to Shoulder Injury

Greater tuberosity.text: The greater tuberosity is the supraspinatus (and posteriorly, infraspinatus) insertion and sits directly beneath the coracoacromial arch; focal tenderness here localizes the mechanical conflict to the subacromial tendons/bursa rather than a more proximal or distal structure.
Greater tuberosity.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

findings: Resisted abduction reproduces the painful arc
Pain only on RESISTED abduction = contractile (tendon) source
Pain also on PASSIVE abduction = inert (bursa) source
sttt.interpretation: Painful only on RESISTED abduction points to a contractile (tendon) source; pain also on PASSIVE abduction points to an inert (bursa) source.

cpa.pattern: Serratus Anterior and Lower Trapezius inhibition drive the scapular dyskinesis; also check Pec Minor overactivity. Fascial component (from source): Pec-minor & posterior-capsule tightness limiting scapular upward rotation.

kineticChain.name: Scapulohumeral Rhythm Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect "Upper trap dominant" or "Serratus deficit, medial winging" (2:1 GH:scapular ratio disrupted), directly narrowing the subacromial space.

functionalScreen.name: Active Flexion / Overhead Reach + Shoulder Abduction Arc
functionalScreen.note: Combined scapulohumeral-rhythm and subacromial screen, with the arc test isolating the painful-arc zone. FMA source note: Scapular-assist / retraction test eases the arc; overhead reach.

Painful mid-arc.text: The same 60–120° compression zone as impingement, but here reflecting tendon-specific load intolerance from reactive or degenerative matrix disorganization within the tendon itself rather than isolated bursal irritation.
Painful mid-arc.source: Cook & Purdam, Continuum Model of Tendon Pathology; JOSPT CPG, Shoulder Pain

minimal wasting.text: Tendinopathy is a matrix-disorganization and pain-inhibition process, not a structural tear, so gross muscle bulk is largely preserved — distinguishing it on inspection from the marked wasting seen with a full-thickness tear.
minimal wasting.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

tender cuff insertion.text: Localized tenderness at the tendon-bone junction reflects nociceptor sensitization within tendinopathic tissue, consistent with an insertional (enthesis) source of pain.
tender cuff insertion.source: Cook & Purdam, Continuum Model of Tendon Pathology

Rounded-shoulder posture increasing suba.text: A protracted scapula with increased thoracic kyphosis raises sustained tensile and compressive load on the rotator cuff tendons during overhead tasks, a recognized mechanical driver of cuff tendinopathy that sits on the same continuum as impingement.
Rounded-shoulder posture increasing suba.source: JOSPT Clinical Practice Guidelines, Shoulder Pain

Greater tuberosity.text: Reproducing pain by direct palpation at the tendon insertion (rather than diffusely) is consistent with Cyriax's principle of localizing a contractile lesion by combining palpation with a painful resisted test in that muscle's line of pull.

findings: Resisted abduction strong but painful
Resisted ER strong but painful (Cyriax minor-lesion pattern)
Passive ROM full and painless
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted abduction and ER is the Cyriax minor-lesion (tendon) pattern; full painless passive ROM rules out a capsular restriction.

cpa.pattern: Infraspinatus/Teres Minor pain-inhibition with Anterior/Posterior Deltoid compensating. Fascial component (from source): Deep-front-arm-line tension; infraspinatus fascial tightness.

kineticChain.name: Scapulohumeral Rhythm Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: Same upper-trap-dominant, serratus-deficit pattern as impingement, since tendinopathy and impingement sit on the same mechanical continuum.

functionalScreen.name: Shoulder Abduction Arc
functionalScreen.note: The painful-arc test is the direct functional correlate of tendon irritability under load. FMA source note: Load-and-shift / resisted-hold reproduces pain, not weakness.

S03.name: Rotator Cuff Tear (Full-Thickness)
keyExams: Full-thickness cuff tests: ER lag, Drop-Arm, Lift-Off
posture: Cannot maintain scapular set under load

Visible supraspinatus/infraspinatus wast.text: Visible hollowing of the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae reflects denervation and disuse atrophy with fatty infiltration of the torn tendon's muscle belly — a reliable sign of an established, chronic full-thickness tear rather than an acute tendinopathy.
Visible supraspinatus/infraspinatus wast.source: Goutallier classification of rotator cuff fatty infiltration; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment

drop of the arm.text: Inability to control eccentric lowering of the abducted arm past roughly 90° reflects loss of the cuff's role as a dynamic humeral head depressor and decelerator; this positive Drop-Arm finding has low sensitivity (~21–27%) but high specificity (~88–96%) for a full-thickness tear, so a positive result is strongly confirmatory even though a negative one does not rule it out.
drop of the arm.source: McGee, Evidence-Based Physical Diagnosis; Physiopedia, Drop Arm Test

Cannot maintain scapular set under load.text: With the cuff's dynamic humeral-centering function lost, the scapular stabilizers and deltoid must substitute for the missing force couple, producing an inability to hold a stable scapular position once the arm is loaded — the postural corollary of the 'combined pattern' (upper-trap dominance plus serratus winging) seen on scapulohumeral rhythm testing.
Cannot maintain scapular set under load.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

findings: Resisted abduction/ER weak & painful (partial tear) or weak & painless (complete rupture)
Drop-Arm/lag signs positive — confirms the major-lesion pattern
sttt.interpretation: Weak & painful = partial tear; weak & painless = complete rupture. Positive Drop-Arm/lag signs confirm this is a major-lesion (structural) pattern, not a minor tendinopathy.

cpa.pattern: Complete inhibition of Infraspinatus/Teres Minor suggesting possible tear; check Subscapularis (lift-off) too, with Anterior Deltoid/Teres Major overcompensating. Fascial/structural component (from source): Cuff atrophy; loss of dynamic humeral centring.

kineticChain.name: Scapulohumeral Rhythm Assessment

fields.label: Scapulohumeral rhythm pattern
options: Combined pattern — upper-trap dominance + serratus winging

kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect the "combined pattern" (upper-trap dominance + serratus winging together), reflecting established, more severe dyskinesis.

functionalScreen.name: Active Flexion/Overhead Reach + Apley Scratch
functionalScreen.note: Cross-check with Apley Scratch for overall reach loss.

S04.name: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)
observation: Global loss of active AND passive motion
posture: Compensatory scapular hitching / trunk lean on reach

Global loss of active AND passive motion.text: Equal restriction of active and passive range is the hallmark distinguishing a true capsular restriction from a muscular/tendinous one, where passive range typically exceeds active; it reflects genuine fibrotic shortening of the capsule and rotator interval rather than pain-guarding alone.
Global loss of active AND passive motion.source: Cyriax, Textbook of Orthopaedic Medicine (capsular pattern concept)

arm held guarded.text: Protective positioning close to the trunk reflects pain provoked by any capsular stretch during the acute 'freezing' (painful) phase of adhesive capsulitis.
arm held guarded.source: Neviaser & Neviaser, staging of adhesive capsulitis

Compensatory scapular hitching / trunk l.text: With true glenohumeral motion restricted in a pan-directional (capsular) pattern, functional reach is achieved by substituting scapulothoracic elevation and trunk lean for the missing glenohumeral excursion — a recognized compensatory strategy in frozen shoulder.
Compensatory scapular hitching / trunk l.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

findings: All resisted tests strong & painless (rules out contractile lesion)
Passive ER/Abd/IR all restricted proportionally (ER>Abd>IR)
Capsular end-feel on passive testing
sttt.interpretation: The textbook Cyriax capsular pattern: proportional restriction ER>Abd>IR with a capsular end-feel, and painless resisted testing ruling out a contractile lesion.

cpa.pattern: Not primarily a compensation pattern — this is capsular fibrosis — but Anterior Deltoid/Upper Trapezius are often overactive compensating for the globally restricted joint during reach. Fascial component (from source): Capsular / axillary-fold fascial contracture; pan-directional restriction.

kineticChain.name: Glenohumeral Internal Rotation (GIRD) Assessment

fields.label: GIRD finding
options: Severely restricted (<30°), all planes restricted (capsular pattern ER>Abd>IR)

kineticChain.chainEffect: Severely restricted (<30°), all planes restricted (capsular pattern ER>Abd>IR)... Adhesive capsulitis likely.

functionalScreen.name: Apley Scratch Lower (IR)

fields.label: Apley Scratch Lower (IR) reach
options: Restricted to L1–L5 or below buttock

functionalScreen.note: The functional correlate of severe GIRD. FMA source note: Every functional reach (hair, back-pocket) globally limited.

S05.name: AC Joint Pathology
observation: Step deformity / swelling over the AC joint

Step deformity / swelling over the AC jo.text: A visible or palpable step reflects superior displacement of the distal clavicle relative to the acromion following disruption of the AC and/or coracoclavicular ligaments, graded by severity using the Rockwood classification of AC joint injury.
Step deformity / swelling over the AC jo.source: Rockwood classification, AC joint separation; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment

tender apex.text: Tenderness localized precisely to the joint apex, rather than diffusely across the shoulder, pinpoints the AC joint itself as the pain generator.
tender apex.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

Protracted shoulder loading the joint.text: A protracted, forward-carried shoulder girdle increases compressive and shear load transmitted across the AC joint during arm use, aggravating an already irritated joint.
Protracted shoulder loading the joint.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

AC joint.text: Direct palpation over the joint line reproducing focal pain is one of the most sensitive individual clinical findings for AC joint pathology, distinguishing it from a subacromial or glenohumeral source.

findings: Resisted GH tests generally painless (non-contractile at the GH)
Passive horizontal adduction reproduces localized AC pain
sttt.interpretation: A joint-play/passive test — not a resisted-muscle one — is what reproduces the pain here, localizing the lesion to the AC joint rather than the GH musculature.

muscles.name: Upper Trapezius / Pec Minor
muscles.state: Tightness increases AC joint compressive load

cpa.pattern: Not a classic muscle-compensation pattern (local joint), but Upper Trap/Pec Minor tightness can increase AC joint compressive load. Fascial component (from source): Deltotrapezial fascia over AC joint.

kineticChain.reason: Not a chain-cascade condition (local AC joint) — Scapulohumeral Rhythm may still show compensatory guarding but isn't diagnostic here.

functionalScreen.name: Shoulder Abduction Arc
functionalScreen.note: Pain specifically AT THE TOP of the arc (full 180°) — rather than the mid-arc 60–120° zone — is the AC-joint-specific finding on this same functional test.

Tender bicipital groove.text: Tenderness overlying the intertubercular (bicipital) groove localizes pathology to the long head of biceps tendon as it courses through the groove — the classic site of biceps tendinopathy and a frequent secondary irritant in impingement.

no wasting.text: Biceps tendinopathy and SLAP lesions are overuse/tendon-labral pathologies without denervation, so muscle bulk remains preserved on inspection.
no wasting.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

Anterior shoulder carriage.text: A humerus held anteriorly/internally rotated increases mechanical irritation of the long head of biceps tendon both within the groove and at its origin near the superior labrum.
Anterior shoulder carriage.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

Bicipital groove.text: Reproducing pain by direct palpation at the groove, typically with the arm positioned in ~10° internal rotation to bring the groove anteriorly, is the classic Cyriax localization test for long head of biceps tendinopathy.

findings: Resisted elbow flexion (biceps LH) strong but painful at the bicipital groove — classic contractile pattern
Resisted shoulder flexion also reproduces groove pain
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted testing localizing to the bicipital groove is the classic Cyriax contractile-lesion pattern for the long head of biceps.

cpa.pattern: Biceps is often overactive AS A COMPENSATOR for an inhibited rotator cuff, so check Infraspinatus/Subscapularis facilitation too. Fascial component (from source): Deep-front-arm line (biceps-coracoid) tension.

kineticChain.reason: Not primarily a chain-cascade condition (local tendon/labral) — Scapulohumeral Rhythm can be checked as an adjunct if impingement co-exists.

functionalScreen.name: Active Flexion + Apley Scratch (if catching)
functionalScreen.note: A catching sensation on Apley Scratch during rotation suggests a labral component. FMA source note: Resisted elevation / O'Brien functional load, catching with rotation.

Apprehension guarding.text: A fear/guarding response — rather than pure pain — when the shoulder is placed in the abduction-external-rotation 'apprehension' position reflects the patient's subconscious anticipation of the humeral head subluxing anteriorly, the behavioral correlate of anterior capsulolabral insufficiency.
Apprehension guarding.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter (Apprehension/Relocation Test)

possible sulcus sign.text: Inferior humeral head translation on a caudal pull (graded I <1cm, II 1–2cm, III >2cm) indicates laxity of the superior glenohumeral ligament and rotator interval; it frequently co-exists with anterior instability as part of a broader multidirectional laxity pattern, and persistence of the sulcus with the arm externally rotated implicates a lax rotator interval specifically.

Loose posture.text: A generally lax, poorly-set shoulder girdle posture often reflects underlying generalized ligamentous laxity, a recognized predisposing factor for glenohumeral instability.
Loose posture.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

scapular dyskinesis.text: Altered scapular positioning reduces glenoid concavity-compression, the dynamic stabilizing mechanism that normally centers the humeral head on the glenoid, compounding the static capsuloligamentous laxity that defines instability.
scapular dyskinesis.source: Kibler, Scapular Dyskinesis and Its Relation to Shoulder Injury

findings: Resisted tests usually strong/painless unless a secondary tendinopathy exists
Passive ER at 90° abduction may show EXCESSIVE range with a soft/hypermobile end-feel
sttt.interpretation: Excessive passive ER with a soft/hypermobile end-feel is the opposite of a capsular restriction — pointing toward instability rather than adhesive capsulitis or OA.

cpa.pattern: Subscapularis inhibition with Pec Major compensating is the exact documented finding for anterior instability. Fascial component (from source): Anterior capsule laxity / global ligament laxity screen.

kineticChain.name: Glenohumeral Internal Rotation (GIRD) Assessment

fields.label: GIRD finding
options: Excessive range / soft end-feel (mirror image of frozen-shoulder finding)

kineticChain.chainEffect: Here checking for EXCESSIVE range/soft end-feel rather than restriction — the mirror image of the frozen-shoulder finding.

functionalScreen.name: Apley Scratch Upper (ER)

fields.label: Apley Scratch Upper (ER)
options: Excessive ER reach with apprehension near end-range

functionalScreen.note: Anterior instability often shows excessive ER reach with apprehension near end-range. FMA source note: Apprehension/relocation in function, feeling of "coming out".

Acutely held rigid.text: In the acute resorptive phase, calcium hydroxyapatite crystals trigger an intense inflammatory response that produces severe, chemically-mediated pain forcing the patient to hold the limb almost motionless — distinct from the mechanical, movement-related pain of impingement.

marked guarding.text: Protective muscle splinting minimizes any movement that would compress or stretch the acutely inflamed calcific deposit and surrounding bursa.

often no wasting.text: The presentation is acute and chemical/inflammatory rather than a chronic structural or denervation process, so muscle bulk is typically preserved even though pain and guarding are severe.
often no wasting.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

Antalgic protective posture.text: The arm is held adducted and supported against the trunk to minimize subacromial compression on the acutely inflamed supraspinatus deposit, the same biomechanical rationale as protective postures in other acute irritable shoulder conditions.

findings: Resisted abduction acutely strong but severely painful (irritable contractile pattern)
Passive ROM markedly guarded/painful in the acute phase
sttt.interpretation: An irritable contractile pattern in the acute phase — strong but severely painful resisted testing plus guarded passive ROM — is consistent with an acute calcific deposit.

cpa.reason: Not classic CPA territory acutely (calcific/chemical irritation) — defer Supraspinatus/Infraspinatus facilitation testing until pain allows. Fascial component (from source): Supraspinatus tendon focal tenderness.

kineticChain.name: Scapulohumeral Rhythm Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: Expect acute guarding producing a pseudo-frozen-shoulder rhythm rather than a fixed motor-control fault.

functionalScreen.name: Active Flexion/Overhead Reach

fields.label: Active Flexion / Overhead Reach
options: Marked painful restriction of active elevation

functionalScreen.note: Consistent with the acute irritable phase. FMA source note: Marked painful restriction of active elevation.

Reduced arm swing.text: Diminished passive and active glenohumeral excursion during functional movement reflects the global capsular thickening and articular restriction characteristic of degenerative joint disease, rather than a localized soft-tissue lesion.
Reduced arm swing.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

muscle bulk loss.text: Disuse atrophy develops secondary to chronic pain-limited use of the joint over months to years, mechanistically distinct from the acute denervation atrophy that follows a rotator cuff tear.
muscle bulk loss.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

possible crepitus.text: Palpable or audible crepitus during motion reflects loss of articular cartilage with roughened subchondral bone-on-bone contact, a hallmark physical sign of glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

Guarded elevated-shoulder posture.text: Chronic joint pain and capsular restriction drive a protective, elevated shoulder-girdle posture that minimizes glenohumeral loading during standing and functional activity.
Guarded elevated-shoulder posture.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Shoulder chapter

findings: Resisted tests generally painless unless a secondary cuff lesion co-exists
Passive ER/Abd/IR restricted proportionally (capsular)
HARD/bony end-feel
sttt.interpretation: A HARD/bony end-feel on proportional capsular-pattern restriction distinguishes OA from adhesive capsulitis, which has a softer capsular end-feel.

cpa.pattern: Anterior Deltoid/Upper Trap often overactive compensating for globally restricted, painful GH motion. Fascial component (from source): Global capsular fascial restriction.

kineticChain.name: Glenohumeral Internal Rotation (GIRD) Assessment

fields.label: GIRD finding / end-feel
options: Restricted — soft capsular end-feel (adhesive capsulitis, for comparison)

kineticChain.chainEffect: Same capsular-pattern restriction as adhesive capsulitis, but with a HARD/bony rather than soft capsular end-feel.

functionalScreen.name: Apley Scratch Lower (IR)

fields.label: Apley Scratch Lower (IR)
options: Restricted — crepitus / bony quality at end-range

functionalScreen.note: Same test as adhesive capsulitis, but expect crepitus/a bony quality at end-range rather than a soft capsular stop.

Neck-driven guarding.text: Protective positioning driven by cervical mechanosensitivity or neural tension — rather than a local shoulder lesion — signals that the true pain generator is proximal, at the cervical spine or brachial plexus.
Neck-driven guarding.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Cervical/Shoulder differentiation

dermatomal signs.text: Sensory change following a specific dermatomal distribution, rather than a peripheral-nerve or myotomal pattern local to the shoulder, points to cervical nerve root involvement as the source of the 'shoulder' symptoms.
dermatomal signs.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.3 (dermatome/myotome differentiation)

Forward-head posture.text: Forward head posture increases compressive and foraminal-narrowing load at the lower cervical segments (C5–C7), the same mechanism that produces referred 'shoulder' pain via cervical radiculopathy (cross-reference Cervical C02).

findings: Shoulder resisted tests typically painless/normal strength — rules OUT a local shoulder lesion
Cervical resisted tests / Spurling's reproduce the pain
sttt.interpretation: The key differentiator: normal shoulder resisted testing plus a positive cervical provocation (Spurling's) confirms this is not a shoulder problem, but a cervical referral.

cpa.pattern: An overactive-scalenes/DNF-inhibition pattern is the driver here, not a shoulder muscle. Fascial component (from source): Neural (brachial plexus) upper-limb tension bias.

kineticChain.name: Cervicothoracic Junction (C7–T4) Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: CT junction hypomobility with arm symptoms is a real alternate driver of "shoulder" pain, via brachial-plexus tension or first-rib elevation.

functionalScreen.reason: Not a shoulder-region functional test — use Cervical AROM Screen + ULNT1 instead (see the STTT/CPA findings above). FMA source note: Neck movement / Spurling's reproduces the shoulder pain.
